title: Kesh as acceptance
hookLine: uncut hair as trust in the body as given

cards: A small wooden comb, curved, with fine teeth, tucked into a knot of hair at the top of the head. That's the kangha, and it's there for kesh, hair that is never cut.
A whole economy runs on changing how we look: trims, dyes, straighteners, filters on photos. Into that world, a Sikh walks with hair left as it grew, wrapped under a turban or a scarf.
From outside, it can look like a rule about appearance. Sikhs tell it another way: a body left as it was given.

teach.b: Day three met kesh under the turban, and day one hundred thirty-nine said start where you are; today goes deeper. First, what kesh is.
It's uncut hair, and for Sikhs who have taken amrit, the Khalsa initiation, it's one of the articles of faith they keep.
The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, names cutting the hair among the things an initiated Sikh must not do.
Other Sikhs keep their hair without having taken amrit, and some don't keep it; the gurdwara door is open to all of them. Second, a phrase from the Granth.

teach.h: SABAT SURAT: THE FORM KEPT WHOLE.
teach.b: In a hymn in Raag Maru, Guru Arjan describes a life of true devotion in the language of his Muslim neighbors, and one of his images is sabat surat: the form kept whole, with the turban on the head. Whole. Not edited.

Sikh teaching speaks of hukam, the divine order, and Guru Nanak's Japji says that by that order forms come into being. If the body came through that order, then leaving it uncut is a way of saying: I accept this as given.
Not a better version. This one. Fourth, acceptance isn't neglect.
The same tradition that keeps the hair uncut gives it a comb. Kesh is washed, combed, oiled, wrapped with care, and the turban is tied fresh.
That's acceptance, not giving up: you don't fight the body or abandon it; you tend what you were given.
Maybe the hardest idea here: the thing you'd most like to change about yourself could be met with a comb instead of a blade.

how: Sikhs who keep kesh leave their hair uncut, comb it with a kangha, and cover it, men usually with a turban and women with a turban or a scarf; initiated Sikhs keep it as one of the articles of the Khalsa.

o: a haircut style worn only on holy days
hair grown long to show a person's rank
uncut hair, kept as trust in the body as given

games.q: kesh as acceptance: tap the pairs.

s: kesh is mainly a rule about looking a certain way
Sikhs tell it as trust in the body as given, kept whole and cared for.
keeping hair uncut means leaving it uncared for
kesh comes with a comb: washed, combed and wrapped.
Guru Arjan speaks of keeping the form whole, with the turban on the head
sabat surat, in a hymn in Raag Maru.

games.q: you're keeping your hair uncut, and a friend asks why you don't just tidy it up with a trim. which answer fits the tradition?
o: it's the body as given, kept whole and cared for.
games.why: Sikh teaching ties kesh to the body as given by the divine order, kept whole, and tended with a comb.

practice: Bring to mind one part of your body you've argued with, your hair, your height, a scar, a knee that complains on the stairs, and if it's easy to reach, rest a hand on it.
Breathe in and let it be there without the argument; breathe out and say quietly, or only in your mind: as given. You don't have to love it today; just stop fighting it for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Kesh as acceptance. Uncut hair, kept whole and cared for, as trust in the body as it was given. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kes, uncut hair, kept by Sikhs as an article of faith.

carryVoice: Your line: as given. Washed, combed, wrapped with care, and left whole. See you again tomorrow.
